proof:
# Weighted three centroid tails and an all-size nested-endpoint theorem

Let K be a full-dimensional convex body in R^d, let g be its ordinary
volume centroid, and let u!=0. Normalize its directional cap function by

    F(s)=|K intersect {u.(x-g)>=s}|/|K|,
    Gamma=gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d.

Then for every s>=0,

    F(0)+F(s)+(1/2)F(-s)>=Gamma+1/2.                (1)

The constant is sharp: take a simplex and a centroid direction with
F(0)=Gamma, then choose s beyond both directional support endpoints.
The other two tails are respectively zero and one.

The proof below includes both affine-power orientations and a negative
central-threshold regularization before localization. Direct application
of localization to the central closed CDF is not valid: its value at a
Dirac mass at zero would be too large. The regularization explicitly
removes that issue.

The all-size consequence is: if A is ANY measurable subset of K of
volume a, then for every real t,

    |K intersect {u.(x-g)>=0}|
      +|A intersect {u.(x-g)>=t}|
      +|K intersect {u.(x-g)>=-t}|
        >=Gamma |K|+a/2.                           (2)

For convex A, (2) supplies a single middle-fiber point controlling all
ambient caps of the actual three fibers A,K,K. It is a restricted
family theorem, not a general mixed-integer proof or a rule for adding
many pairs while reusing the same middle-fiber contribution.

## 1. Scalar form and the Dirac-safe localization

For d=1 the body is an interval, so F(0)=1/2 and F(s)+F(-s)=1.
Thus the left side of (1) is 1+F(s)/2>=1=Gamma+1/2.
Assume d>=2. The centered scalar marginal is nonatomic and 1/d-concave
as a probability measure; its density has concave (d-1)-st root.
This is the ordinary Brunn--Minkowski marginal statement.

Write G(t)=P[u.(X-g)<=t]. All its points are atomless. Inequality (1)
is equivalent to

    G(0)+G(s)+(1/2)G(-s)<=2-Gamma.                 (3)

If s=0, Grunbaum and Gamma>1/3 give
F(0)+F(0)+F(0)/2>=5Gamma/2>=Gamma+1/2.
Hereafter s>0. If (3) were strictly violated, nonatomicity implies that
for some sufficiently small 0<epsilon<s it would remain violated with
G(0) replaced by G(-epsilon).

On a fixed compact interval containing the marginal support, use the
one-constraint localization theorem of Fradelizi--Guedon, Theorem 2,
with probability-concavity parameter 1/d<=1/2 and the constraint

    integral x dnu(x)>=0.

The objective is now the affine upper-semicontinuous functional

    Phi_epsilon(nu)=nu((-infinity,-epsilon])+nu((-infinity,s])
                     +(1/2)nu((-infinity,-s]).       (4)

All three half-lines are closed relative to the fixed interval.
An admissible Dirac mass is located
at x>=0. It contributes to at most the middle term in (4), so its
value is at most 1<2-Gamma. In particular the Dirac at ZERO is harmless.

The theorem therefore reduces a hypothetical violation to a non-Dirac
extremizer with mean exactly zero and density proportional to a
nonnegative affine function raised to the power d-1 on an interval.
For each such density Phi_epsilon<=Phi_0. It suffices to prove (3)
with its unshifted central term for ALL these centered affine-power
laws. Sections 2--5 do so.

The localization theorem, its precise hypotheses, and the same
one-sided mean constraint were independently checked in
`candidate 732b11a769399016`, Section 2.
The primary references are [the author-hosted paper](https://perso.math.u-pem.fr/fradelizi.matthieu/pdf/localizationDCG.pdf)
and [the author-uploaded full text](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220452814_The_Extreme_Points_of_Subsets_of_s_-Concave_Probabilities_and_a_Geometric_Localization_Theorem).
Only the ordinary one-constraint theorem is used here. The limiting
argument epsilon decreasing to zero is applied to the ORIGINAL
nonatomic law, not to a Dirac extremizer.

## 2. The increasing affine-power family

After an affine change, its density is

    f(t)=d t^(d-1)/(1-r^d),  r<=t<=1,  0<=r<1,
    G(t)=(t^d-r^d)/(1-r^d) on [r,1], clipped to [0,1].

Its mean m and its central CDF p are

    m=d/(d+1) * (1-r^(d+1))/(1-r^d), p=G(m).       (5)

We will use

    (1+r)/2<=m<1,           Gamma<=p<=1/2.          (6)

The mean is at least the interval midpoint by pairing the increasing
density at equidistant points. Grunbaum gives p>=Gamma: this law is
the first-coordinate marginal of a convex frustum with cross-sections
tL, where L is any (d-1)-dimensional convex body. Alternatively, the
concavity proved in Section 4 gives g(R)>=Gamma+(1-Gamma)R and hence
p=(g(R)-R)/(1-R)>=Gamma directly. For the upper bound,
its quantile q(v)=(r^d+(1-r^d)v)^(1/d) is concave. Hence
m=integral_0^1 q(v)dv<=q(1/2), so p<=1/2.

Put c=2m-1>=r and T_r=G(c). The already proved paired-centroid-tail
theorem in the cited companion note implies

    T_r<=1-2Gamma.                                 (7)

Indeed at shift 1-m the upper tail is zero and the opposite tail
is 1-G(2m-1); their sum is at least 2Gamma. This uses a result already
proved independently, not the weighted theorem currently being shown.

If the ORIGINAL law has this increasing density, then

    F(0)+F(s)+(1/2)F(-s)
      =1-p+1-G(m+s)+(1/2)[1-G(m-s)].              (8)

While 0<=s<=1-m, its derivative is
-f(m+s)+(1/2)f(m-s)<0. After s=1-m the upper-tail term is zero
and the remaining variable term is nondecreasing until constant.
Thus its minimum occurs at s=1-m and equals

    1-p+(1/2)(1-T_r)
       >=1-1/2+(1/2)(2Gamma)=Gamma+1/2.            (9)

This completes one orientation in every d>=2, using exactly (6)--(7).

## 3. All shifts in the decreasing orientation

Reflect the law in Section 2 about its mean. Its upper tails are
F(s)=G(m-s), and the expression of interest is

    p+J(s),   J(s)=G(m-s)+(1/2)G(m+s).              (10)

Let

    k=2^(-1/(d-1)), A_d=[2/(1+k)]^(d-1),
    s_*=m(1-k)/(1+k).                              (11)

On 0<=s<=1-m both arguments lie in the support, by (6). The derivative
J'(s)=-f(m-s)+(1/2)f(m+s) changes sign exactly once, from negative
to positive, at s=s_*. On 1-m<=s<=m-r the upper CDF is one and
J is nonincreasing; afterwards J=1/2. Consequently:

* If s_*>1-m, the global minimum is 1/2.
* If s_*<=1-m, the global minimum is min{J(s_*),1/2}.

These alternatives include equality of the two critical shift values.
The constant branch gives p+1/2>=Gamma+1/2 immediately. In the other
branch, both critical thresholds are inside the support and

    m-s_*=2km/(1+k), m+s_*=2m/(1+k)<=1.

Since k^(d-1)=1/2, direct substitution gives

    p+J(s_*)=[(1+A_d)m^d-(5/2)r^d]/(1-r^d).        (12)

It remains to bound (12) whenever m<=(1+k)/2.

## 4. Concavity of the powered truncated mean closes the critical branch

Write R=r^d and alpha=1/d. The mean in (5) satisfies

    m(R)=integral_0^1 [R+(1-R)t]^alpha dt,
    g(R)=m(R)^d.

The function g is CONCAVE on [0,1]. Here is a direct proof. On (0,1),
put a=R+(1-R)t, I=integral a^alpha, A=integral a^(alpha-1)(1-t),
and B=integral a^(alpha-2)(1-t)^2. Differentiating g=I^(1/alpha) gives

    g''=(1-alpha)I^(1/alpha-2)(A^2-I B)<=0,

by Cauchy--Schwarz. Continuity extends this concavity to both endpoints.
No concavity assertion about the original marginal CDF is being made.

The mean m(R) increases continuously and strictly from d/(d+1) to 1.
The number (1+k)/2 lies strictly between these endpoints. To check
the first strict inequality, with p_0=d-1>=1, Bernoulli gives
(1+2/p_0)^p_0>=3>2 and hence k>p_0/(p_0+2).
There is therefore a unique R_* in (0,1) with

    m(R_*)=(1+k)/2.

The critical branch of Section 3 is exactly 0<=R<=R_*. Define

    H(R)=(1+A_d)g(R)-(Gamma+1/2)-(2-Gamma)R.         (13)

It is concave. At R=R_*, the critical shift equals 1-m. The exact
expression (12) becomes p+G(2m-1)+1/2, at least Gamma+1/2.
Thus H(R_*)>=0.

At R=0, g(0)=Gamma, so H(0)=A_d Gamma-1/2. This is nonnegative,
indeed strictly positive, by the elementary constant bound proved in
Section 5. Concavity now gives H(R)>=0 on the WHOLE interval [0,R_*].
By rearrangement, this is exactly the desired bound for (12).
Both orientations of every nonconstant affine-power law are proved.
Constant affine densities are centered uniform interval laws; their
weighted expression is at least 1 and hence at least Gamma+1/2.
Together with Section 1 this proves (1).

## 5. An elementary bound for the dimensional constant

For d=2, A_d Gamma=(4/3)(4/9)=16/27>1/2.
For d>=3 put p_0=d-1>=2. Monotonicity of positive power means gives

    A_d=[2/(1+2^(-1/p_0))]^p_0
        >=[2/(1+2^(-1/2))]^2
        =8/(3+2 sqrt(2))>15/11.                    (14)

For completeness, power-mean monotonicity here is just Jensen applied
to x^(2/p_0), a concave function, at the two numbers 1 and 1/sqrt(2),
followed by taking the relevant positive powers and reciprocals.
The last strict inequality in (14) is equivalent to 43>30 sqrt(2),
whose square is 1849>1800.

Also Gamma>1/e>11/30. One elementary rational bound for the latter is

    e=sum_(j=0)^infinity 1/j!
      <65/24+(1/120)sum_(j=0)^infinity (1/6)^j
      =1631/600<30/11.

The tail estimate is strict because after the fifth factorial term
the successive denominator factors eventually exceed six. Finally
(1+1/d)^d<e, for example by d log(1+1/d)<1. Thus (14) proves
A_d Gamma>(15/11)(11/30)=1/2. The same bound implies Gamma>1/3,
used at zero shift and below.

## 6. A measurable subset and two identical large fibers

Restore V=|K| and write F for UNNORMALIZED cap volume in this section.
For any measurable A subset K of mass 0<=a<=V,

    |A intersect {u.(x-g)>=t}|>=max{0,a-V+F(t)}.     (15)

For fixed t, subtract a/2 from the proposed sum in (2). As a function
of a in [0,V], the lower bound furnished by (15) is decreasing until
a=V-F(t), and increasing afterwards. Its minimum there is

    F(0)+F(-t)+(1/2)F(t)-V/2.                       (16)

If t<=0, inequality (1) with s=-t bounds (16) below by Gamma V.
If t>=0, the already proved paired-tail inequality and monotonicity
give instead

    F(0)+F(-t)+(1/2)F(t)
      =F(0)+(1/2)[F(t)+F(-t)]+(1/2)F(-t)
      >=(5/2)Gamma V >=(Gamma+1/2)V,

since F(-t)>=F(0)>=Gamma V and Gamma>1/3. This proves (2) in every
dimension d>=1. All cut hyperplanes are volume-null; measurable A
inherits that nullity, so all displayed bounds apply to closed caps.

Now let A itself be a convex body contained in K. The convex hull of
the three fibers A,K,K at bases -1,0,1 has exactly those fibers, because
(A+K)/2 subset K. Any nonvertical cap through the actual point (0,g)
has continuous thresholds t,0,-t in those three fibers. Equation (2)
proves its mass is at least Gamma V+a/2. A vertical closed cap contains
the whole middle K, and has mass 2V or V+a, also above that bound.
Containing caps include parallel through-point caps. Consequently

    depth_S((0,g)) >= (Gamma V+a/2)/(2V+a)
                       >= Gamma/2.                (17)

This includes every size a<=V, arbitrary shapes, and every oblique
ambient halfspace. The point is the ordinary centroid of the middle
fiber; it need not be the true mixed centroid.

The same conclusion holds when the two large fibers B,C are translates
of the same K. A permitted integer shear makes them identical. The
midpoint inclusion then forces the transformed small fiber inside K:
h_A+h_K<=2h_K implies h_A<=h_K in every direction. Thus this is an
actual geometric extension, not a density replacement.

Each use of (2) includes the middle term F(0). It cannot be summed over
many endpoint pairs while charging that term only once. No such global
allocation is assumed or proved.

## 7. A common core, and every nested three-fiber chain

Suppose the actual three convex fibers at bases -1,0,1 are A,B,C.
Assume there is a full-dimensional convex body K with

    A subset K,       K subset B intersect C.

Set a=|A|, V=|K|, and E=|B|+|C|-2V>=0. Applying (2) to the
two copies of K contained in B,C shows that every nonvertical cap
through (0,g_K) has actual mass at least Gamma V+a/2. Vertical
through-point caps contain either B+A or B+C. Their masses are at
least V+a or 2V, respectively, so the same lower bound holds. Thus

    depth_S((0,g_K)) >= (Gamma V+a/2)/(2V+E+a).     (18)

In particular this is at least Gamma/2 whenever

    E <= (1/Gamma-1)a.                             (19)

All quantities in (18) are volumes of the original fibers or of the
specified common core; no measure replacement is asserted.

This proves OC for EVERY three-fiber family totally ordered by set
inclusion. Indeed, the midpoint inclusion (A+C)/2 subset B and
Brunn--Minkowski prohibit B from being a strict smallest member of
that chain: if both endpoints contain B and one contains it strictly,
their midpoint body's volume exceeds |B|. Equal-volume nested convex
bodies coincide. After reversing the base if necessary, the smallest
fiber is therefore an endpoint A. Let K be the smaller of B,C, let
V=|K|, and let W be the larger volume; then a<=V<=W.

If W-V>=a, the largest fiber has mass at least half the total and
its ordinary centroid alone gives mixed depth at least Gamma/2.
If W-V<a, use (18) with E=W-V. Since Gamma<=1/2,

    E<a<=(1/Gamma-1)a,

so (19) applies. This includes ties: if all three bodies coincide,
choose either endpoint as A. The selected point is always at an
actual integer base, and every oblique and vertical closed cap has
been accounted for. The statement also holds after any permissible
affine transformation or affine-in-base continuous shear which makes
the three fibers a nested chain.

The arithmetic signs, concavity derivative identity, and subset
optimization are independently checked in
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_weighted_three_centroid_tails.py`. Earlier bounded screens are
not dependencies of this proof.
